data center power is not one thing - important to delineate the multiple bottlenecks causing power delays 

1. getting power to the site is about interconnect (grid) or behind the meter (renewables, nuclear, gas plant)

2. power outside the data hall is about transformers (voltage step down), generators or batteries for redundancy, ATS (auto transfer switch) to toggle between the two sources, and switchgears which transfer medium voltage power to a second transformer in the data hall which steps down voltage again

3. power inside the data hall is the UPS (uninterruptible power supply which can handle brief power outages until generator comes online), PDUs (power distribution units) which are basically power strips on steroids within the rack, and the PSU (power supply unit) which converts and feeds the right voltage to the rack, and lastly the VRM (voltage regulation monitor) which fine tunes and stabilizes the power to the CPUs and GPUs

each of these steps in the data center power flow has immense structural shortages and needs re-design to accommodate denser racks and higher power compute.  so "power" is really about a number of things with very different profiles, value chains, etc.

if you read @CrucibleCap's Data Center Report on Power Systems, Cooling, and the Switch to 800V DC in Feb 2026, you'd be miles ahead of the curve 😉

we've invested in critical infrastructure in each of these layers of the data center power stack, from materials to power electronics to orchestration and optimization tools to financial engineering tools to manage volatility and risk

Most agent failures today are really memory failures.

The model is usually capable enough. What’s missing is the graph around you: who your wife is, who your closest friends are, how you know someone, what you last discussed, which channel you use with them, recurring context, preferences, commitments, etc.

Most systems build memory slowly through nightly “dreaming” over your conversations. That creates a nasty cold-start problem: the agent needs days or weeks of interaction before it actually knows you well...

And even then, many systems store memory as a flat pile of facts instead of maintaining a proper person-level memory layer. Muse does this better: you can effectively end up with wife.md, best_friend.md, coworker_x.md aka persistent context for each important person.

You can bootstrap this yourself today. Give a local agent access to your iMessage, WhatsApp, email and calendar history on your computer and ask it to:

"resolve identities across channels
cluster messages/events by person
infer relationships and recurring topics
rank people by recency + frequency + reciprocity
generate one Markdown memory file per person, with timestamps and evidence"

It may take hours over a large corpus, but you skip the cold start entirely and end up with hundreds of high-quality person-specific memories on day one. That makes every downstream agent dramatically less context-blind. 

Then you can give the memories files to your preferred agent. @nikunj gave me the idea yesterday to look more at my local data (he has his own killer agent system)
